articles.title: Pa. Gov. Josh Shapiro’s popularity and ‘get sh-t done’ attitude might not cut it in crowded 2028 Democratic field – but he has options
articles.dek: The 2026 midterm elections swept Democrats into office around the country in such numbers that journalists were running out of synonyms for “ massive .”
paragraphs: The 2026 midterm elections swept Democrats into office around the country in such numbers that journalists were running out of synonyms for “ massive .”

In Pennsylvania, Gov. Josh Shapiro won reelection by 22 percentage points, winning more than 60% of the vote – something that has been accomplished only twice before in the modern era in the Keystone State.

Not only did Shapiro wipe the floor with his opponent Stacy Garrity, the state treasurer, but he also helped flip four U. S. House seats from red to blue. His coattails benefited down-ballot candidates , helping Democrats solidify their control of the state House and flip the state Senate as well .
Shapiro’s political stock in Pennsylvania is riding high.

I’m a political science professor and political media researcher in central Pennsylvania, and many of my former students work in Harrisburg. Some are Democrats working for or around the governor; others are Republicans working in different corners of state government. All are finely tuned to the political gossip that swirls around a successful politician whose star is on the rise. It is the worst-kept secret in American politics that Josh Shapiro wants to be president.

I’ve met the governor a handful of times and can attest to his George Clooney-level charisma. He’s a hard worker, has maintained a remarkably clean political profile, and is from many accounts a genuinely nice dude.
And yet, there are plenty of reasons his ambitions may require some careful timing, regardless of his personal strengths.

Shapiro’s political victories didn’t just happen. Over the past four years, he has worked to demonstrate bipartisan competence as Pennsylvania’s chief executive, adopting an expression he uses frequently: “ get sh-t done .”
Now, with Democrats holding the governor’s office and both chambers of the General Assembly, Shapiro told reporters : “We got the power now, the House, the Senate. We have to deliver.”

Shapiro’s approval ratings have remained strong , consistent with his reelection margins. That’s unusual in a state that has swung back and forth between supporting Donald Trump in 2016 , Joe Biden in 2020 and Trump again in 2024 , each time by fewer than 2 percentage points.
If Shapiro is indeed seriously eyeing the White House , his current popularity will certainly serve him well. But winning the presidency is an enormous undertaking, particularly in a crowded field.

With Trump unable to run in 2028, the next presidential election will feature open seats for both parties and likely attract many candidates. Democrats, in particular, have a deep bench of attractive potential contenders .

There are so many possibilities that Shapiro could find himself running against people very much like him: younger centrists, swing-state politicians and accomplished elected officials with solid records. Consider just a few names that could be part of the conversation: Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker and former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel.

Shapiro would have to find a way to distinguish himself in a field filled with candidates who can make many of the same arguments about their experience, political appeal and accomplishments. That’s a tall order. A Plan B might be wise.

He could run for the Senate in 2028 against incumbent John Fetterman, if Fetterman seeks reelection . This would be a twofer: Shapiro would continue his rise in politics, and he would likely beat a guy he apparently does not like. The two reportedly don’t speak , much less get along.

Shapiro could also position himself for a vice presidential nomination by attaching himself to another 2028 hopeful. This would buy him time to build his national profile, allow the presidential field to sort itself out and potentially put him in a strong position for another run at the White House down the road. It would also give him an opportunity to demonstrate that he can work effectively on a national stage.

Or he could angle for a Cabinet post. The federal government has undergone significant restructuring under DOGE and Trump’s executive orders. Should a Democrat win the White House in 2028, rebuilding federal agencies and restoring institutional capacity will be a monumental undertaking. Shapiro could be an attractive candidate for a major administrative role.

The bottom line for Shapiro is that he will need to distinguish himself from a crowded field of Democrats by emphasizing his statewide victories in a major swing state, impressive fundraising ability and a political voice that can evoke Barack Obama without alienating either his party or the broader electorate. That’s a tricky feat, even for the most talented politicians.

But Nov. 3, 2026, showed us that he knows how to make sh-t happen. Whatever he decides, the next two years will be important for Shapiro, consequential for Democrats, and fascinating for political scientists like me, who will be watching events unfold with a keen eye and, probably, a bucket of popcorn.

articles.title: Students creating documentaries with scientists deepens STEM belonging and public trust in science
articles.dek: Marine scientists navigate autonomous glider robots across the Atlantic Ocean and along the West Antarctic Peninsula , collecting data to help predict storm intensity.
paragraphs: Marine scientists navigate autonomous glider robots across the Atlantic Ocean and along the West Antarctic Peninsula , collecting data to help predict storm intensity.
When farmers’ fields are destroyed by an unknown pathogen, plant scientists spend years breeding new varieties of disease-resistant food crops.
A team of microbiologists explore deep-sea volcanoes in search of organisms that may contain anticancer compounds.

These are passionate people who are dedicated to seeking solutions to real-world problems. They are also the main characters in science documentaries produced in the Rutgers Immersive Learning Science Storytelling Lab that I oversee. Our lab pairs students with working scientists to co-create documentaries about research as it happens, while earning experiential learning credit.
At a time when confidence in science is declining , I was approached by scientists who wanted their authentic research stories communicated to broad audiences.

I am an educator, a researcher and anthropologist , and a science filmmaker who has been making science documentaries with Rutgers students and researchers since 2008. The science-in-action storytelling model I developed is intended to make the human journey of science visible to the public. Our stories communicate the process, motivations and integrity behind science, which helps earn public confidence and trust in science .

I also partner with STEM learning researchers to gauge whether our documentaries increase the relatability of scientists, increase public understanding of scientific processes and help students find belonging in STEM.
Science-in-action storytelling is composed of five steps that support student-scientist relationships.
First, the storytellers develop trust with the participating university scientists. This trust stems from shared respect and a mutual understanding of the co-creation process.
The scientists then invite storytellers into their labs and field sites, where we capture their research processes in real time. This is Step 2.

Our professional storytelling team, which includes students, then documents scientists conducting research, including experiments and data collection, as they describe the why and how of their work. Depending on the complexity of the project, we collect dozens to hundreds of hours of science-in-action video footage.

Importantly, this video data is maintained in our storytelling lab, as it often includes recordings of federally funded research. Maintaining the video data repository is a key component to establishing and sustaining trust with the participating scientists.

Step 3 invites students to immerse themselves in the video data and begin shaping the footage into documentary scenes, constructed using only the scientists’ words, without narration. As they analyze hours of footage, our students learn about the authentic scientific processes; in doing so, they participate in research through the process of storytelling.
Our students are not graded on their documentary skills, nor are they required to make a film. Instead, they are graded on the science they learn through the storytelling process.

Step 4 requires that the students share drafts of their documentary scenes with the featured scientist to verify the accuracy of the science communicated. This step is part of the foundational trust agreement with the scientists but is also an opportunity for the students to personally connect with scientists.

For Step 5, our lab works to distribute the documentaries to a wide variety of audiences, including the general public. Here we partner with STEM learning experts to assess audiences’ understanding of and trust in the science communicated in the film and audience perceptions of the featured scientists.

Our completed science-in-action documentaries have reached audiences far beyond the university. Our National Science Foundation-funded “ Antarctic Edge: 70° South ” had a theatrical release and aired on Netflix. “ Atlantic Crossing ” was broadcast on PBS stations and was included in a three-year Smithsonian exhibit . “ Fields of Devotion ” was shared by the Association of American Universities as part of its campaign to increase public trust in science . And our lab’s newest long-form documentary, “ Mysteries of 9° North ,” co-created with 14 undergraduates and featuring scientists studying life at deep-sea volcanoes, will be released to the public in early 2027.

Our surveys capture how these science documentaries change audience understanding of science and how it is done. For example, after screening “ Antarctic Edge ,” viewers’ self-reported understanding of climate change rose from 71% to 91% . On a 15-item knowledge quiz, average scores rose, with gains of up to 24 percentage points on the concepts they knew least about.

When 102 undergraduates were asked what made the scientists in “ Fields of Devotion ” relatable, they named passion for the subject (72%), desire to help others (71%) and commitment to their work (70%).

Our survey results also suggest that students who participated in the lab gained confidence and feelings of belonging in a science community. Undergraduates who once said they did not feel “smart enough” reported that they could now see themselves as scientists . All participating students reported that their collaboration with scientists positively transformed their understanding of science.
Nonscience majors gained a deep understanding of the scientific process, while science majors gained rare access to research outside their own disciplines.

Student-directed science documentaries include “ Growing the Caribbean Glider Fleet ,” featuring scientists monitoring hurricane development; “ Biting Back: The Lifesaving Potential of Catnip ,” about the development of natural insect repellents; “ Where Waters Meet on the Breathing Shore ,” featuring climate scientists studying coastal ecosystems; “ The B. A. S. I. L Project ,” about USDA-funded plant-breeding research; “ Ocean Farming ,” about NOAA supported oyster breeding; “ The Women of Nsongwe ,” about USAID-supported agriculture projects in Zambia; and “ Skycatcher ,” about an NSF-funded atmospheric chemistry study in Alabama.

This science-in-action model offers a path forward that other universities could follow. Institutions can strengthen students’ STEM learning and science identities while training a new generation of credible, relatable voices for science.
Uncommon Courses is an occasional series from The Conversation U. S. highlighting unconventional approaches to teaching.

articles.title: Democrats’ agenda will be set by their ability to organize and compromise — not by the socialist, progressive or centrist factions all claiming victory
articles.dek: The massive Democratic majority in the U. S. House and Senate that was ushered in by a historic blue midterm vote is an ideologically diverse one .
paragraphs: The massive Democratic majority in the U. S. House and Senate that was ushered in by a historic blue midterm vote is an ideologically diverse one .

Candidates spent much of the past year differentiating their positions from the mainstream Democratic coalition. The result is a freshman class filled with as many progressive liberals as moderate problem solvers .

By the morning after Election Day, pundits and current Democratic members across the political spectrum were quick to claim their ideologically aligned candidates as the “ majority makers ” – the group most responsible for the large victory.
Centrist Democrats pointed to pragmatic moderates flipping Trump-won seats. Liberal voices highlighted the enthusiasm and turnout driven by a new, progressive vision.
As a result, days after the election the focus had turned toward January: Who will become the majority maker within Congress?

Party caucus leaders have already started building their roster : The Progressive Caucus claims at least 25 new members in their ranks, growing their membership to over 100 Democratic members. The moderate Blue Dog Caucus doubled in size , from 10 to 20 new members. And in the middle, the center-left New Dems are projecting a caucus of over 140 members.

I’m a political scientist who has worked in and now studies Congress . Figuring out the dynamics and direction of the 120th Congress requires looking at more than the ideological positions of the candidates who won. Instead, focusing on the number of candidates who won can provide insight into the direction of the party as a whole.

The large – and at the time of writing, still growing – margins of Democratic control in the 120th Congress are the biggest since 1993 , before Congress became consistently competitive and increasingly polarized. Those large margins provide essential context for understanding how this new ideological coalition will work in Congress.

While history demonstrates that an ideologically diverse party can be hard to wrangle , the size of the new Democratic majority provides some breathing room for policy negotiation and procedural debates.

Unlike the current Republican Caucus that is reliant on keeping historically narrow majorities together to pass party goals, future Democratic leadership can stand to lose a few votes. With a minimum of 254 seats in the House and 54 seats in the Senate , small-scale Democratic defections are irrelevant.
This breathing room provides the potential for negotiation, while also limiting any mandate an ideological group may claim.

For instance, the 120th Congress will have eight members in the House who are backed or affiliated with the Democratic Socialists of America , known as the DSA. In raw terms of political power, when the majority has at least 36 votes to spare on any given party-line bill, this group may not matter in policymaking.

If a group – say, the entirety of the Progressive Caucus’ 100-plus membership – decides to stick together, leadership will be forced to listen. Thus, the potential power of ideological factions depends not only on their ideas but their own organizational skills.

When groups in Congress develop practices such as confidential meetings or binding rules that require members vote together on certain votes, the legitimacy of group demands can be strengthened. This is a strategy that has been employed with relative success by the far-right Republican Freedom Caucus since it was formed in 2014.
The overarching policy goals for newly elected Democrats are consistent across the ideological spectrum: lowering the cost of living and rooting out corruption.

This was highlighted in acceptance speeches by Democrats from South Carolina to Texas to Michigan . All emphasized the same policy-focused promise: Instead of fighting left versus right, the fight should focus on the top versus the bottom.
This shared vision is no doubt important. My research has shown that a cohesive message is a key part of winning and maintaining majority control.

However, the “blue tsunami” was powered by voters with very specific policy demands. And as is always the case with policymaking, the details matter. Does healthcare reform mean reinstating the Obamacare subsidies set to expire on Jan. 1, 2027? Or does it mean something bolder, such as Medicare for All ?
While there is power in numbers, the organizational strength and ultimate success of ideological groups in Congress depends on how unified they can be around specific policy goals and proposals.
This means that who is doing the unifying also matters.
The success of any potential legislative package heavily relies on congressional leaders’ knowledge of congressional rules and their willingness to incorporate member viewpoints.

This necessity of having leadership in place to get legislation moving is epitomized by the order of operations for a new congressional session. In the coming weeks, both parties will hold closed-door, secret-ballot elections to select their new party leaders . That’s well before any legislation is even drafted.

With a Democratic caucus filled with anti-establishment candidates across the ideological spectrum, and external pressure from political pundits to dump current Democratic leadership , the future of the Democratic Party has been projected onto this otherwise ritualistic vote .

But the power and success of congressional leadership lies in its procedural acumen, not its ideological vision. Some already in Congress have noted New York Democratic Rep. Hakeem Jeffries’ experience and working relationships in discussions of whether he should be house speaker. Furthermore, groups can extract concessions during leadership selection in exchange for their support, such as seats on powerful committees or an agreement on policy agenda items.

articles.title: NASA to Welcome Expedition 74 Astronauts Home at Space Center Houston
articles.dek: NASA will welcome home the Expedition 74 crew during a public event at Space Center Houston following their return from a long-duration mission aboard the International Space…
paragraphs: NASA will welcome home the Expedition 74 crew during a public event at Space Center Houston following their return from a long-duration mission aboard the International Space Station.

NASA astronauts Jessica Meir, Jack Hathaway, and Chris Williams; ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Sophie Adenot; and Roscosmos cosmonauts Sergey Kud‑Sverchkov and Sergei Mikaev will share mission highlights at 6 p. m. CST Tuesday, Nov. 17, at NASA Johnson Space Center’s visitor center. An awards ceremony recognizing key mission contributors will follow the presentation.

The astronauts will be available for media interviews before the event. Media may request an in-person interview no later than 5 p. m. Monday, Nov. 16, by emailing the JSC Newsroom at jsc-newsroom@mail. nasa. gov .

Williams, Kud‑Sverchkov, and Mikaev launched aboard the Soyuz MS-28 spacecraft from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan on Nov. 27, 2025. The trio returned to Earth on July 26, making a parachute-assisted landing southeast of Dzhezkazgan, Kazakhstan. The crew was in space for 241 days, orbiting the Earth 3,856 times and traveling more than 102 million miles. The mission was the first for Williams and Mikaev and the second for Kud-Sverchkov.

Meir, Hathaway, and Adenot launched aboard a Dragon spacecraft on Feb. 13 as part of NASA’s SpaceX Crew-12 mission from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. After more than seven months aboard the space station, Meir, Hathaway, and Adenot safely splashed down on Oct. 8 in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of Los Angeles.

During their 237-day mission, the four crew members traveled more than 100 million miles and completed more than 3,792 orbits around Earth. The mission was the second for Meir and the first for Hathaway and Adenot. Roscosmos cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev also flew as part of Crew-12 but is unavailable for the event.

The Expedition 74 crew dedicated more than 1,400 hours to scientific research and technology demonstrations aboard the International Space Station. Its work advanced in-space manufacturing by testing metal and tissue 3D-printing technologies and supported human health studies examining the effects of long-duration spaceflight. Research included blood flow studies, assessments of piloting capabilities under changing gravitational conditions, and activation of a new compact exercise system . The crew also evaluated life-support and environmental systems critical to future exploration missions under NASA’s Artemis program.

In addition, the crew members conducted pharmaceutical research to crystalize proteins for cancer medications , advance tumor targeting treatments , and grow stem cells for therapeutics. They cared for the first set of plants studied outside of curated systems , upgraded an instrument used to advance our understanding of matter and develop new quantum technologies, managed visiting spacecraft, and performed essential maintenance to support the continued operation of the orbiting laboratory.

Beyond research and operational achievements, Expedition 74 engaged students and audiences around the world through live educational events, outreach activities, and the sharing of stunning imagery that highlights the importance of scientific discovery and international collaboration in space.

For more than 26 years, people have lived and worked continuously aboard the International Space Station, advancing scientific knowledge and making research breakthroughs not possible on Earth. The space station helps NASA understand and overcome the challenges of human spaceflight, expand commercial opportunities in low Earth orbit, and build on the foundation for long-duration missions to the Moon, as part of the Artemis program, and to Mars.
Learn more about International Space Station research and operations at:

articles.title: NASA Scientists Show How Gravitational Waves Can Reveal New Worlds
articles.dek: The LISA (Laser Interferometer Space Antenna) observatory, now in development, will detect gravitational waves, the tiny ripples in space-time caused by orbiting masses.
paragraphs: The LISA (Laser Interferometer Space Antenna) observatory, now in development, will detect gravitational waves, the tiny ripples in space-time caused by orbiting masses. Now two studies led by NASA astrophysicists show in new detail how LISA could reveal a new and unique population of exoplanets — worlds beyond our solar system — throughout our galaxy.

“The most common source for LISA is expected to be double white dwarf systems, which are binaries composed of white dwarfs in tight orbits,” said Casey McGrath, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County and NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland. “If an exoplanet also orbits within one of these systems, its presence becomes imprinted on the gravitational wave signal in a way we’ll be able to uncover.”

Two papers published Tuesday in The Astrophysical Journal detail the findings. The first , authored solely by McGrath, examines the detection method and determines the planet masses and orbital periods where it would work best. The second paper , by McGrath and coauthors, investigates how such planets could be confirmed using NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope .
The possibility of detecting exoplanets around LISA double white dwarf systems was first proposed by Japanese astronomer Naoki Seto in 2008.

Led by ESA (European Space Agency), the LISA mission is slated for launch in the mid-2030s. As a collaborative partner, NASA is contributing the telescopes, other critical hardware, and engineering and scientific support as part of its mission to better understand how the universe works.

The LISA detection method is similar to one called radial velocity that uses light and is already employed to find exoplanets around nearby stars. As a planet orbits, its gravity tugs on its host star, imparting a small reflex motion, or wobble, onto it. This wobble causes the star’s spectrum to oscillate, with spectral lines shifting from redder wavelengths as the star moves away from us to bluer ones as the star moves toward us. The shift is due to a phenomenon called the Doppler effect .

“Something similar occurs with gravitational waves,” said Scott Noble, a theoretical astrophysicist at NASA Goddard and a coauthor on the confirmation paper. “By themselves, double white dwarfs will emit gravitational waves at a nearly continuous frequency. Add a sufficiently massive planet to the system, and its presence causes the binary to experience reflex motion, adding a Doppler modulation to the gravitational signal.”
For LISA, this modulation will appear as sidebands, secondary signals at both higher and lower frequencies than the primary one.

McGrath likens the situation to modern radio communication, where some of the energy of a main radio carrier frequency goes into forming sidebands at adjacent upper and lower frequencies that carry messages (like voices or music). For gravitational waves, the sidebands carry messages about the presence of a planet.

White dwarfs are the Earth-sized remnants of stars like the Sun. While exoplanets have been detected around a few isolated white dwarfs, none have yet been found around a binary white dwarf, which means the LISA detections would represent a distinct new exoplanet population.

Astronomers estimate that our Milky Way galaxy contains 10 million double white dwarf systems with orbital periods of less than an hour, which generate gravitational waves in the right range for LISA to find. They expect LISA will resolve about 10,000 individual systems, as well as around 100 mixed binaries — with white dwarfs, neutron stars, or black holes — orbiting in similar periods.

“Once LISA captures its first exoplanet detections, it will be critical for us to validate some of them,” said Mary Anne Limbach, an assistant research scientist at the University of Michigan and a co-author on the confirmation paper. “These joint detections will allow us to establish that the gravitational signals correspond to genuine planets rather than false positives.”

The team described a new method for confirming these planets by taking advantage of the Webb telescope’s infrared sensitivity. A planet in a double white dwarf system produces a larger portion of infrared light than what’s expected from the stars themselves. Webb’s instruments can easily detect this infrared excess out to a distance of at least 500 light-years.

articles.title: Autumn Mornings Bring Valley Fog
articles.dek: On a cool November morning, low clouds traced the branching valleys of the Appalachian Plateau and the Cumberland River.
paragraphs: On a cool November morning, low clouds traced the branching valleys of the Appalachian Plateau and the Cumberland River. By afternoon, they had faded, leaving clear skies over the autumn landscape.

The change is visible in this pair of images from November 8, 2026. The MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) on NASA’s Terra satellite acquired the left image that morning. In this natural-color view, low clouds appear white as they fill many of the valleys. Autumn vegetation appears in shades of brown and green.

The VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) on NOAA-21 acquired the right image that afternoon, after the clouds had dissipated and exposed the rivers and lakes beneath them. This false-color view makes it easier to distinguish water (dark blue) from vegetation (bright green).

The clouds appear to be fog, a type of cloud that forms near the ground . Foggy mornings in the region are common this time of year. As nights lengthen, the ground has more time to radiate away the day’s heat, and the air just above it cools to the dew point —the temperature at which air becomes saturated and water vapor begins condensing into the tiny droplets that make up fog.

Because cold air is denser than warm air, it flows downslope and pools in valleys, so fog tends to form there first. Notice the fog filling the branching valleys across part of the Appalachian Plateau in eastern Kentucky and southwestern West Virginia. Rivers and streams that run along many of the valley floors add to the effect by supplying extra moisture. The same pattern is visible along the Cumberland River and its reservoirs in north-central Tennessee and south-central Kentucky.

According to the National Weather Service, temperatures in many places on the morning of November 8 dipped into the 30s Fahrenheit before giving way to a mild, sunny afternoon. Forecasters reported locally dense valley fog that morning. Dense fog had also blanketed a wider part of the region earlier in the week, prompting advisories for hazardous travel conditions.

articles.title: Curiosity Blog, Sols 5056-5062: Charging Back Up!
articles.dek: By Remington Free, Operations Systems Engineer, NASA-JPL
paragraphs: By Remington Free, Operations Systems Engineer, NASA-JPL

Today’s plan covered 3 sols, 5060, 5061, and 5062, as we take a few recharging sols before getting back to our normal drilling activities. As you may know if you have been following the blog closely, we are in the middle of a drilling campaign on our target called “Nazca.” We’ve already drilled the hole, characterized the tailings from the drill hole with ChemCam, and have now done several sample dropoffs, both to our SAM and CheMin instruments within the belly of the rover. We still have a number of activities left to do as part of the campaign, including another dropoff to SAM for a different kind of analysis, and drilling cleanup activities.

One of those activities is called “RAGE” (Rotate to Agitate for Granule Expulsion, a very fun acronym) where we essentially shake the drill to get any remaining sample out of it. We’ll also make sure to take lots of imaging to continue document the drill hole and tailings.

In any case, those activities are very power-hungry for our rover! So today’s plan purposefully did not have a lot of activities in it so we could get a nice few power positive sols before we get back to drilling. Each of our three sols had a standard morning science block, with an extra exciting brand-new activity on 5061 (more on that shortly! ).

Over the three sols, we conducted remote science with ChemCam active and Remote Micro-Imager mosaics on some interesting targets (“Titicaca,” “Pampas,” and “Salta”), some Mastcam imaging of our calibration target and our drill target, several Navcam dust devil studies and Mastcam tau observations, and twilight imaging. Despite this plan being recharging/waiting, we got in lots of exciting science to continue to study the Nazca crystal formations and the nearby layered rocks and bedrock.

On 5061, we also conducted a brand-new engineering activity to test parallelism over one of our downlink communications windows. articles.title: Curiosity Blog, Sols 5050-5055: It’s Nazca, Our 49th Drill Hole
articles.dek: Written by Susanne P. Schwenzer, Professor of Planetary Mineralogy at The Open University, UK
paragraphs: Written by Susanne P. Schwenzer, Professor of Planetary Mineralogy at The Open University, UK

As regular readers of this blog will know, we returned to the area where we found disc shaped inclusions in the rocks, which we interpreted as potential crystals. If they are indeed crystals, and we compare them to Earth, they could be very interesting indicators of the environmental conditions. Hence, the excitement in the team is high that we found a good block to drill. Good means first and foremost that it contains abundant potential crystals, but of course there is more before we drill. We passed the rover’s stability test, as all wheels have to be on solid ground before we extend the arm.
Then we passed the preload test, which tests the stability of the rock and the forces the arm experiences when the drill bit presses into the rock.
With all those tests passed, we successfully drilled our 49th drill hole, called “Nazca.”

The drill campaign comes with many investigations before and after the drilling itself. Before the drill, we investigated the block with APXS, MAHLI and ChemCam – all on the target Nazca. After drilling, the sample was dropped off to CheMin, with the results still making their way from Mars to Earth. They are eagerly anticipated to reach us over the coming weekend. ChemCam obtained both passive spectral and active LIBS of the tailings and a LIBS measurement down the drill hole wall.

Other ChemCam activities this week included a LIBS investigation of “Palpala,” which is a dark pebble. We are on the lookout for those pebbles for a while and find that not all of them have the same composition. To make sure we understand their origin, we are measuring them when there are some in reach that are big enough. If a pebble is too small, it can move when it is being hit by the laser. Hence, we need to look out for some that are big enough.

Another such pebble was the target “Puna” identified in Friday’s planning. ChemCam LIBS on the target “Llama” is to get another depth profile to check whether our observations in the first such depth profile are consistently observed or whether they vary between locations.

The target “Pacaya” is another measurement of the disc shaped forms that drew us back to this region. In addition to the LIBS measurements, ChemCam has several long distance RMIs in the plan. They are all focused on the two buttes that have drawn a long-standing interest of the team for the various sedimentary structures and textures they reveal: Mishe Mokwa and Cordillera.
